# witness-spec

**The fleet's witness log, with a standard canonicalisation, domain
separation, and the external anchor it never had.**

The house's witness machine — `recorder.py` in `AI-Writings`,
`witness/ledger.js` in `quilt-claw`, `ledger.js` and `ledger.rs` across
the fleet — is the fleet's most-repeated idiom and its most-repeated
*blind spot*. Three findings, all measured here:

## 1. The canonicalisation is a house convention, and it diverges

The chain hashes `fnv1a64(json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True,
separators=(",", ":")))`. Every port reimplements that by hand. It is not a
standard, and it differs from **RFC 8785 (JCS)** in three measured ways:

```
house:  {"x":1.0,...}          ->  "x": 1.0        JCS:  "x": 1
house:  {"\ue000":2,"\ud800\udc00":1}   JCS:  {"\u{10000}":1,"\uE000":2}
house:  "é"                    ->  "é"    JCS:  "é"
```

**The key-order row is the dangerous one.** JCS sorts object keys by
**UTF-16 code units**; Python's `sorted()` sorts by **code point**. They
disagree for any key above U+FFFF against one below. A chain hashed in
Python and a chain hashed in JavaScript would diverge on such an object —
silently, and only on the keys nobody was looking at.

**RFC 8785 is a `MUST` in A2A v1.0 §8.4.1**, so adopting it is also the
interoperable choice.

## 2. The chain is ATTESTABLE, not tamper-evident

This is the finding that matters, and `test/tamper.test.mjs` demonstrates
it rather than asserting it:

> **A hash chain is self-consistent, and self-consistency is not
> tamper-evidence.** Rewrite a record, re-chain it, and the chain verifies
> perfectly.

The test builds a log, edits a record, re-chains it, and shows that
`verify()` returns `ok: true`. The rewrite is **indistinguishable from the
original**. The house's ledger has no external anchor, so it has no
tamper-evidence at all.

**Truncation is the same defect, and it is cheaper to exploit.** Delete the
last 50 records of a 121-record `witness-chain/1` log and the remaining 71
replay cleanly — `verify()` returns ok, and the head just moves. *A
truncated chain is a shorter valid chain.* No re-hash, no fixpoint
iteration, no competence required.

The fix is the standard shape (RFC 6962 / Trillian's `LogWitness`): a
periodic **signed tree head** under a key the log writer does not hold.
The same test then shows the rewrite **detected**, because the head
changed and the signature no longer matches.

**And the hash is FNV-1a-64.** That is 64 bits and not collision-resistant.
An attacker rewriting a chain does not need to collide anything — they just
recompute. SHA-256 costs nothing and is already in every runtime here.

**One domain-separation byte** (`0x00` leaf, `0x01` node, RFC 6962 §2.1) and
**one signed head, published out of band**, turn a log that is merely
*self-consistent* into a log that is *tamper-evident*.

Publication is not a detail of the anchor design; it **is** the anchor. A
signature over a head stored inside the log it anchors is a signature the
writer can refresh for free after every rewrite and every truncation.

## 2a. The three legs, and a verdict that says which it has

A log earns the word *tamper-evident* only when all three hold:

| # | leg | who in the fleet has it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **chain re-derives** — replay reproduces every linkage | every chained log |
| 2 | **head signed** by a key we trust | `doubt-ledger` (`sign_root`, optional), `moth-ledger` (`Ed25519Signer`, opt-in, not on the write path) |
| 3 | **head published out of band** — where the log writer does not control it | **nobody. zero repos.** |

Leg 1 alone is **attestable**. Legs 1+2 are **attested**. Only 1+2+3 is
**tamper-evident**. As of this commit the fleet is at leg 1 everywhere, so
the correct word is *attestable* — narrower, and true.

### Linkage class — `chain` vs `row-checksum` vs `none`

A chain and a row-checksum log are **different objects**, and the fleet has
been calling both of them "witness". `SPEC.md` makes this normative: every
verdict emits a linkage class, and the class decides the words it may use.

| linkage class | catches | cannot catch |
|---|---|---|
| `chain` | edit, reorder, drop-in-the-middle | tail truncation; a re-chained rewrite |
| `row-checksum` | bit-rot, partial corruption | deletion, truncation, reordering |
| `none` | — | — (refused with a reason, never silently skipped) |

This is load-bearing, measured: **`bots/*/witness.log` are row-checksum
logs wearing a chain's name.** Ten of them, **0 carrying a `prev` field**.
Delete 50 rows from `rsi-gan`'s 262 and the surviving 212 still self-verify.
A verdict on one of those may say *"row checksums match"* and must name the
class — **it may not say "intact"**, because a set of independent row
checksums has no linkage to be intact with respect to. A `chain` verdict may
say **"chain-intact"**, meaning precisely: the chain verified.

## 3. The cross-language byte-identity claim is now checkable against a
standard

`conformance/vectors.json` holds four records chosen to cover exactly the
cases that diverge: a float that must become an integer, a negative zero, a
control character, a non-ASCII character, keys on **both** sides of the BMP
boundary, and a nested array.

**The JavaScript and Python reference implementations reproduce every
canonical form, every leaf hash, every chain hash, the head, and the
signature — byte for byte.** That is measured, not asserted: the Python
twin re-derives the vectors from the spec, and the vectors are what proves
the two agree. They are not transcriptions of each other.

```
$ node test/all.mjs
running 1 test file(s)
# tests 6
# pass 6
```

## The spec

`SPEC.md` — the chain rule, the three additions and why each is needed,
the migration (this **changes every hash**, so it is a format change and
ports must refuse a version they do not implement), and what is **not**
claimed.

## Licence

MIT.

# witness-chain/1

**The fleet's witness chain, with a standard canonicalisation, domain
separation, and an external anchor.**

Status: draft. The current chain (`FNV-1a-64` over
`json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))`) is what ships
today. This is the replacement, and it is a **format change** — see
*Migration* at the bottom.

## The chain rule

```
canonical(i) = JCS(record_i)                        RFC 8785
leaf(i)      = SHA256(0x00 || canonical(i))          RFC 6962 2.1 domain separation
hash(0)      = GENESIS = 0x0000000000000000
hash(i)      = SHA256(0x01 || hash(i-1) || leaf(i))  RFC 6962 2.1
head         = hash(n)
signature    = HMAC-SHA256(0x03 || head)            under a key the log writer does not hold
```

## Linkage class — a verdict MUST name which kind of log it is looking at

**A chain and a row-checksum log are different objects, and the fleet has
been calling both "witness".** A verdict that does not say which one it is
looking at cannot be read. This section is normative: every verifier emits a
linkage class, and the class determines which words the verdict may use.

| linkage class | test | what it catches | what it CANNOT catch |
|---|---|---|---|
| `chain` | dense `seq` from 0 **and** replay reproduces every linkage | edit, reorder, drop-in-the-middle | truncation of the **tail**; a re-chained rewrite |
| `row-checksum` | each row carries a hash of **its own payload only** | bit-rot, partial corruption | deletion, truncation, reordering — the rows do not commit to each other |
| `none` | neither of the above | — | — |

**Required output.** A verifier emits `linkage: 'chain' | 'row-checksum' | 'none'`
alongside its verdict, and `linkage: 'none'` is a **reported category, not a
silent skip** — a log with no linkage is refused with a reason, never passed over.

**Why the distinction is load-bearing, measured.** The fleet's `bots/*/witness.log`
files are named `witness`, carry a field called `hash`, and are described as
witnessing. **0 of them carry a `prev` field.** The hash is a checksum of the
row's own payload. Deleting 50 rows from `rsi-gan`'s 262 leaves 212 rows that
still self-verify; the deletion is invisible. A row-checksum log is not a chain,
and calling it one borrows the credibility of the idiom without the property.

## Tamper-evidence — the three legs, and which ones you have

The fleet says "tamper-evident" about logs that have one leg out of three.
The honest claim is narrower and more precise; **narrowing a claim is the fix.**

| # | leg | what it means |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **chain re-derives** | replay reproduces every linkage; a rewrite is *expensive* |
| 2 | **head signed** | the head is signed by a key we trust |
| 3 | **head published out of band** | the signed head lives somewhere the log writer does not control |

| legs held | the correct word |
|---|---|
| 1 only | **attestable** — "the chain re-derives" |
| 1+2 | **attested** — "the chain re-derives and the head is signed" |
| 1+2+3 | **tamper-evident** — and only then is the word earned |
| 1, but no linkage | **row checksums match** — never "intact" |

**A verifier MUST NOT use the word "tamper-evident" for a log whose head is not
both signed and published out of band. A truncated chain is a shorter valid
chain.** Tail-truncating a 121-record `witness-chain/1` log by 50 records still
verifies, and the head simply changes to a value nobody holds a signature for.
Leg 3 is the whole of the difference, and leg 3 is the leg nobody has built.

**"intact" is not producible for a row-checksum log.** For a `chain`, the verdict
may say **`chain-intact`** — the chain verified. For a `row-checksum` log it must
say **`row checksums match`** and name the class, because a checksum set has no
linkage to be intact *with respect to*.

## The three things this adds, and why each is needed

### 1. RFC 8785 (JCS) instead of a house convention

The current chain canonicalises with
`json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))`. That is a **house
convention**, reimplemented by hand in every port. It is not a standard,
and it diverges from RFC 8785 in three measured ways:

| input | house convention | RFC 8785 (JCS) | why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| `1.0` | `1.0` | `1` | Python's `repr` vs ECMAScript `Number::toString` |
| keys `\u{10000}` and `\uE000` | `\uE000` first | `\u{10000}` first | **JCS sorts by UTF-16 CODE UNITS; Python's `sorted()` sorts by CODE POINT** |
| `é` | `é` | `é` | Python's `ensure_ascii=True` escapes it |

**The key-order case is the dangerous one.** A chain hashed in Python and a
chain hashed in JavaScript disagree on any object carrying both kinds of
key — silently, and only on the keys nobody was looking at. That is
precisely the class of bug a canonical form exists to prevent, and it is
the class the house's own cross-language byte-identity claim is exposed to.

**RFC 8785 is already a `MUST` in A2A v1.0 §8.4.1.** Adopting it means the
fleet's witness log interoperates with a protocol it wants to speak.

### 2. Domain separation

A leaf and an interior node hash **different bytes** (`0x00` vs `0x01`
prefix). Without it, the bytes of a leaf can be presented as a node, and
the two kinds of thing are not distinguishable. This is RFC 6962 §2.1 and
it is one byte per hash.

### 3. A signed tree head — the external anchor

**A hash chain is self-consistent, and self-consistency is not
tamper-evidence.** Rewrite a record, re-chain it, and the chain verifies
perfectly. The `test/tamper.test.mjs` file demonstrates exactly this, and
the demonstration is the point:

> **WITHOUT an anchor, a rewritten log is indistinguishable from the
> original.** The current ledger has no anchor, so it has no
> tamper-evidence at all — the fleet's most-repeated idiom is its least
> protected one.

**Truncation is the same defect wearing a different hat, and it is worse,
because it needs no competence at all.** An attacker who deletes the last 50
records of a 121-record `witness-chain/1` log leaves 71 records that replay
cleanly; `verify()` returns ok and the head simply moves. *A truncated chain
is a shorter valid chain.* No rewrite, no re-hash, no fixpoint iteration —
just deletion. This is why leg 3 (publication) is not a refinement of the
anchor design but the whole of it: a signature over a head that lives inside
the log it anchors is a signature the writer can refresh for free.

The fix is the standard shape (Trillian's `LogWitness`): a periodic
**signed tree head**, signed under a key the log writer does not hold. The
rewrite changes the head; the head's signature no longer matches.

**The key must not be the log writer's key.** If the writer can sign, the
writer can re-sign, and there is no anchor. The house's witness machine
(`recorder.py`, `witness/ledger.js`, `ledger.rs`, `ledger.js`) needs a key
held by a different party, or at minimum a head published somewhere the
writer does not control.

**The hash is SHA-256, not FNV-1a-64.** FNV is not a cryptographic hash: it
is 64 bits, not collision-resistant, and an attacker rewriting a chain
does not need to collide anything — they just recompute. The chain rule's
*shape* is unchanged, so the port work is mechanical.

## Conformance

`conformance/vectors.json` holds four records chosen to cover the cases
that actually diverge: a float that must become an integer, a negative
zero, a control character, a non-ASCII character, keys on both sides of
the BMP boundary, and a nested array.

**A port conforms when it reproduces every `canonical`, every `leaf`, every
`hash`, the `head`, and verifies the `headSignature`.** The reference
implementations in `ref/` are the JavaScript and Python twins, and the
vectors are what proves they agree — not that they were transcribed from
each other.

```
node test/all.mjs        # 6 tests, including the tamper demonstration
python3 ref/chain.py     # the twin
```

## Migration

**This changes the bytes of every hash.** A log written under
`witness-chain/0` (FNV-1a-64, house canonicalisation) does NOT verify under
`witness-chain/1`, and must not be silently reinterpreted.

1. Write the new chain beside the old one. Do not rewrite history.
2. Record the transition in the ledger: a `CHAIN_VERSION` record naming
   both heads.
3. Ports read the version field and refuse a log whose version they do not
   implement — **a port that cannot answer must be a failure, never a
   value** (the same rule the fold suites already follow).

## What is NOT claimed

- **This is not a fix for the empty-ledger defect.** A chain that is
  written correctly and then not committed is still not evidence. The
  `gitpp-oracle` fix (assert the ledger grew) is a separate matter and
  already shipped.
- **A signed head detects a rewrite; it does not prevent one.** It bounds
  the damage to "the rewrite is visible", and only if the head is
  published somewhere the writer does not control.
- **Nobody in the fleet has built the publication leg.** There is no
  `witness-heads/` in any repo, and no committed `.sig`/`.pub` artifact
  beside any log. `doubt-ledger` ships `sign_root()` (Ed25519, real, and
  correctly refuses rather than degrading when `cryptography` is absent)
  and `moth-ledger` ships an `Ed25519Signer`, but neither writes a signed
  head to a place the log writer cannot reach. Until that exists, the
  correct word for every fleet log is **attestable**, and the anchor is a
  design on paper rather than a property in force.
- **HMAC is a stand-in.** HMAC-SHA256 is symmetric — both parties hold the
  key, so it proves *someone with the key* wrote it, not *who*. Ed25519
  (as in Certificate Transparency, and as Trillian uses) attributes the
  head to a named signer. **Do not ship HMAC as if it were a signature.**

# witness/ — if it wasn't witnessed, it didn't happen

> **This ledger is ATTESTABLE, not tamper-evident.** It has one of the three
> legs an anchor needs. The chain re-derives; the head is not signed; no head is
> published out of band. See *What this ledger does not prove* below — and note
> that deleting the final `OUTCOME` row still makes `--verify` exit 0.

`ledger.jsonl` is an append-only, hash-chained receipt ledger of this repo's test
suite: one record per test file (path, source sha256, tests run), chained, plus one
`OUTCOME` recording the aggregate.

The idiom is ported from `SuperInstance/AI-Writings` → `labs/situation-recorder/recorder.py`.
The hash algebra is **byte-compatible** with it on purpose — same `fnv1a-64`, same
canonical JSON (`sort_keys=True`, compact separators), same
`GENESIS = 0x0000000000000000`, same chain rule:

```
hash = "0x%016x" % fnv1a64( canon({ prev, ...envelope_without_hash }) )
```

It was verified against the Python implementation: 9 canonical-encoding vectors
(key ordering, floats, unicode, astral-plane, control characters) and the chain rule
itself all produce identical bytes. One idiom to invent fewer of.

## Re-derive it

```bash
npm run witness            # rebuild the ledger from live test runs, verify, tamper self-test
npm run witness:verify     # re-derive the chain AND re-run every witnessed file
```

or directly:

```bash
node witness/ledger.js --verify             # full: chain + sha256 + live test counts
node witness/ledger.js --verify --chain-only # fast: chain + sha256 only, no test run
node witness/ledger.js                      # rewrite ledger.jsonl from scratch
```

## What breaks it

All four of these were fault-injected and confirmed to fail:

| tamper | detected by | exit |
|---|---|---|
| edit a test file (append a line) | sha256 drift | 1 |
| delete a test file | missing witness record | 1 |
| add an unwitnessed test file | file count mismatch | 1 |
| hand-edit `ledger.jsonl` | hash mismatch at `seq` | 1 |

These are all **re-derivation** checks. That is a real property and it is
worth having — but it is not the same thing as tamper-evidence, because all
four assume the tamperer does *not* recompute the chain.

## What this ledger does not prove

A log earns the word **tamper-evident** only when all three legs hold:

| # | leg | here? |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **chain re-derives** — replay reproduces every linkage | **yes** |
| 2 | **head signed** by a key we trust | no — nothing is signed |
| 3 | **head published out of band** — where the writer does not control it | no — no published head exists |

This ledger has **leg 1 only**. Two attacks are therefore invisible to it:

- **The re-chained rewrite.** Recompute the chain over your own edit and every
  id agrees, because you recomputed it. The four faults in the table above are
  all *naive* tampers.
- **The tail truncation.** *A truncated chain is a shorter valid chain.*
  Measured here: delete the final `OUTCOME` row — the aggregate verdict for the
  whole run — and `node witness/ledger.js --verify` still prints `CHAIN OK` and
  **exits 0**. Nothing in the file records that the `OUTCOME` ever existed.

So the verdict string says **`chain-intact`**, which means precisely *the chain
verified* — not *nothing was tampered with*. Closing this gap is one build:
sign the head (Ed25519, with a verifier that refuses rather than degrades when
the backend is absent) and commit that signed head somewhere this repo's own
workflow cannot push to.

Normative definitions: [`SuperInstance/witness-spec`](https://github.com/SuperInstance/witness-spec) `SPEC.md`.

## Why this exists

`npm test` used to be `node test/*.test.js`. Node resolves that to the **first**
path and treats the other 26 as `argv` — so it ran `ack.test.js` (4 tests) and
exited 0. A green badge over 4 of 182 tests. Nothing about "tests passed" tells you
how much was tested, which is why the count itself has to be a receipt.

`.github/workflows/test.yml` runs this on every push and PR, and additionally asserts
the count independently via `scripts/assert-suite.mjs` — deliberately a separate
implementation, so a bug in the witness can't quietly pass everything.

Note: the ledger records `tests` counts and `sha256`s, not wall-clock time or the
suite's result, so it stays byte-reproducible. Re-running the builder overwrites it
deterministically.

name: corpus
# The loop guards its own dataset. Every transcript is a hash-chained receipt
# ledger; this gate rebuilds the corpus from committed sources and fails if ANY
# chain does not re-derive — no keys, no network.
#
# WHAT THIS IS: RE-DERIVATION, not tamper-evidence. This gate proves every hash
# re-derives from the committed bodies, which makes a naive edit expensive and
# visible. It cannot see a rewrite that recomputes the chain, and it cannot see
# a tail truncation at all — a truncated chain is a SHORTER VALID CHAIN and this
# gate would pass it. Tamper-evidence needs a signed head published out of band,
# which this repo does not have. The honest word is "attestable".
# (ML-IN-THE-LOOP.md: a naive loop rots; the first guardrail is honest, verifiable data.)
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - "situations/transcripts/**"
      - "situations/dispatch-ledger.csv"
      - "labs/situation-recorder/**"
      - ".github/workflows/corpus.yml"
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - "situations/transcripts/**"
      - "situations/dispatch-ledger.csv"
      - "labs/situation-recorder/**"
      - ".github/workflows/corpus.yml"
jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
      - name: recorder self-test (chain re-derivation + the re-chained-rewrite limit)
        run: python3 labs/situation-recorder/recorder.py
      - name: rebuild + verify the whole corpus (fails on any chain that does not re-derive)
        run: bash labs/situation-recorder/run_all.sh
      - name: assert every transcript chain verifies
        run: |
          python3 labs/situation-recorder/corpus.py >/dev/null
          echo "all transcript chains verified ✓"

# bots/ — and what `witness.log` actually is in here

> **`bots/*/witness.log` are ROW-CHECKSUM logs, not chains.**
> The filename promises a witness; the format does not deliver one. This note
> says which is which, so a verdict about one of these files can be read.

## The measurement

Every `witness.log` in this directory carries the fields
`ts, iso, event, payload, hash`. **None of them carries a `prev` or a
`prev_hash`.** The `hash` is a 16-hex-char checksum of the row's own
payload — it commits a row to itself and to nothing else.

| bot | rows | linkage class |
|---|---|---|
| `rsi-gan` | 262 | `row-checksum` |
| `snowball-scout` | 21 | `row-checksum` |
| `autoclaw-bg` | 14 | `row-checksum` |
| `wesley-mechanic` | 9 | `row-checksum` |
| `bruno-architect` | 8 | `row-checksum` |
| `casper-critic` | 4 | `row-checksum` |
| `jevvy-auditor` | 4 | `row-checksum` |
| `herman-historian` | 2 | `row-checksum` |
| `kira-cartographer` | 2 | `row-checksum` |
| `marcel-composer` | 2 | `row-checksum` |

**10 logs, 328 rows, 0 with linkage.**

A chain is a sequence in which each element's commitment covers its
**predecessor**. These rows do not cover each other, so deleting one leaves
the survivors perfectly valid — there is nothing in a surviving row that
remembers it existed.

Measured on the largest of them: drop the last 50 rows of `rsi-gan`'s 262 and
the remaining **212 still verify**. So does deleting the worst 50 runs. The
checksum catches bit-rot and partial corruption. It catches nothing else.

## What this means for the word "intact"

**"intact" is not producible for a `row-checksum` log.** These rows have no
linkage to be intact *with respect to*. A verdict on one of these files says:

> `262/262 row checksums match` — linkage class `row-checksum`
> — deletion and truncation are **undetectable**; this is not a witness log.

A `chain` verdict may say **`chain-intact`**, meaning precisely *the chain
verified*. That word is not available here.

The honest general word for these files is **attestable** — and even that is
generous, because it implies a chain. What they have is bit-rot detection.

## If a bot wants a real witness log

Write `witness-chain/1` records, using
[`../labs/situation-recorder/recorder.py`](../labs/situation-recorder/recorder.py)
or the spec it implements. Do not keep calling a checksum a chain — the
filename already borrows credibility the format cannot return. And note that
even a proper chain is not tamper-evident until its signed head is published
out of band; see below.

## The house vocabulary

A log earns **tamper-evident** only when all three legs hold:

1. **chain re-derives** — replay reproduces every linkage
2. **head signed** by a key we trust
3. **head published out of band**, where the log writer does not control it

These logs hold **none** of them. `labs/situation-recorder/` transcripts hold
**leg 1 only** and are therefore **attestable**. Nothing in this repo currently
holds leg 3 — there is no `witness-heads/` and no committed signature beside
any log, which is the gap that has to be closed before any log here can be
called tamper-evident.

Normative definition:
[`SuperInstance/witness-spec`](https://github.com/SuperInstance/witness-spec)
`SPEC.md` — *Linkage class* and *Tamper-evidence — the three legs*.

# situation-recorder — the manager↔crew system, saved as a decomposable corpus

*A `labs/` cell. Zero dependencies (Python stdlib). Reusable by any captain/director.*

The fleet's real product is not only the repos a crew ships — it is the **recorded inputs and
outputs of the manager↔crew system**, saved so a future model can learn the one skill this fleet
runs on: take a compound thing apart, locate where the value/truth lives, recombine. This cell is
that capture unit. Design: [`../../situations/arch/INTER-RELATIONAL-INTELLIGENCE.md`](../../situations/arch/INTER-RELATIONAL-INTELLIGENCE.md).

## What it does

Records one **situation** (one manager+crew mission) as an append-only JSONL **receipt ledger** —
the same idiom [`SuperInstance/MicroMoth-quilt`](https://github.com/SuperInstance/MicroMoth-quilt)
uses for quantum circuits: every line a cell, **hash-chained**, replayable. Each line is one
**relation-record** whose `refs` are the graph edges — so a transcript is a *graph of how the parts
related*, not a flat log.

## The chain rule: `witness-chain/1`

The chain rule was upgraded. The old one is **`witness-chain/0`** and is still READ and VERIFIED —
a log that cannot verify its own history is a lie about the past. New records are
**`witness-chain/1`**.

```
v0:  hash = fnv1a64(json.dumps({prev, **envelope}, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")))
v1:  leaf(i) = SHA256(0x00 || JCS(record_i))          RFC 6962 2.1 domain separation
     hash(i) = SHA256(0x01 || hash(i-1) || leaf(i))    RFC 6962 2.1
```

**Why the change, in three parts. The third is the one that matters.**

1. **RFC 8785 (JCS)** instead of the house convention. The v0 canonicalisation was
   `json.dumps(sort_keys=True)`, reimplemented by hand in every port. It is not a standard, and it
   diverges from JCS in three measured ways: `1.0` -> `"1.0"` (JCS: `"1"`); keys are sorted by
   **code point** in Python and by **UTF-16 code unit** in JCS, so they disagree for any key above
   U+FFFF against one below; and Python's `ensure_ascii` escapes non-ASCII where JCS does not.
   RFC 8785 is a `MUST` in A2A v1.0 §8.4.1, so this is interoperability, not pedantry.

2. **Domain separation** — a leaf hashes with a `0x00` prefix and a node with `0x01`, so the two
   kinds of thing cannot be confused.

3. **THE OLD RULE HAD NO TAMPER-EVIDENCE AT ALL.** A hash chain is *self-consistent*, and
   self-consistency is not tamper-evidence: rewrite a record, re-chain it, and the chain verifies
   perfectly, because the attacker recomputed it. v0 also used **FNV-1a-64**, which is 64 bits and
   not collision-resistant, so an attacker rewriting a chain does not need to collide anything —
   they just recompute.

   **Tamper-evidence needs an anchor OUTSIDE the log.** `sign_head()` / `verify_head()` implement
   the standard shape (RFC 6962 / Trillian's `LogWitness`): a **signed tree head**, under a key the
   log writer does not hold, published somewhere the writer does not control.

   **Truncation is the same defect, and it is cheaper to exploit.** Delete the last 50 records of a
   121-record `witness-chain/1` transcript and the remaining 71 verify cleanly — `verify()` returns
   ok and the head simply moves. *A truncated chain is a shorter valid chain.* No rewrite, no
   re-hashing, no competence required. So the **publication** half is not a detail of the anchor
   design, it is the whole of it: a signature over a head stored inside the log it anchors is a
   signature the writer can refresh for free.

   **The key must not be the writer's key**, or the writer can re-sign and there is no anchor.
   HMAC-SHA256 is used because it is in both the Python and the JavaScript standard libraries, but
   **it is a stand-in, not a signature** — it is symmetric, so it proves "someone with the key
   wrote it", not "who". Ed25519 is the production answer.

`recorder.py --out` demonstrates all of it, and the self-test asserts both halves:

```
RE-CHAINED rewrite verifies?           True   <- a chain alone CANNOT tell
RE-CHAINED rewrite caught by the signed head? True
```

The forgery in that demo is a **fixpoint**: it re-chains *and* re-points every `refs` entry that
names a changed hash, because re-pointing a ref changes a record's body, which changes its hash,
which cascades. A forgery that only re-chains is caught by the `refs` check — that is a second
layer of detection, and worth knowing about, but it is only as good as the attacker's care. The
signed head does not depend on the attacker's competence.

### Migration

This changes every hash, so it is a **format change**. `verify()` accepts both versions and
**rejects a chain that MIXES them** — the version is a field inside the record, so it is inside
the hashed bytes and cannot be stripped without breaking the chain. To migrate: **start a new
transcript and name the previous head in it.** Do not rewrite history.

### Cross-implementation byte identity

`SuperInstance/witness-spec` holds the conformance vectors and the JavaScript reference. This
implementation reproduces **every canonical form, leaf hash, chain hash, the head, and the
signature** from them, byte for byte. Three implementations, one chain rule.

```
rel ∈  TASK   dispatcher→captain: the brief (input)
       ROUTE  captain: sub-task → chosen crew/tool + why   (the dispatch policy)
       DRAFT  crew: prompt+params → response                (the generators)
       DRAW   dice: request → un-gameable value + receipt    (forced exploration)
       FOLD   referee: compound claim → leaves, argmin, gap  (decomposition itself)
       KEEP / DROP  captain: candidate + reason              (the value function / label)
       MARK   any: a durable artifact (commit/doc/receipt)
       OUTCOME any (later): realized result                  (the delayed label)
```

The `FOLD` record is the point: it stores the compound claim, every leaf verdict, the **located
weakest** (argmin), and the **gap** between the whole-claim verdict and the folded minimum — the
datum that teaches *how much a single scalar hid.* A corpus of FOLD records is a corpus of
decompositions with their answers attached.

```python
           refs=[d["hash"]])
```

### Drawing the dice with no network (in-environment)

When the Moth API is rate-limited or blocked, get `DRAW` records **locally** with
[`draw_local.py`](draw_local.py) — it builds a MicroMoth-quilt circuit, seals the draw as a
collapse-ledger receipt, self-verifies the chain, and returns `(value, receipt)` you pass straight
to `Situation.draw()`:

```bash

```


**Honest provenance (keeps the corpus clean):** MicroMoth-quilt is a *simulator* — the draw is
quantum-structured and replayable with an attestable receipt (its cell ids re-derive; nothing is
signed and no head is published out of band), but it is **not** a hardware QRNG
and carries no Bell-S. So it's the *throttled-case* dice; reach for the real Moth QRNG when you need
hardware un-gameability, and never launder one as the other. See the first real transcript
[`../../situations/transcripts/sit-2026-09-29-capture-path.jsonl`](../../situations/transcripts/sit-2026-09-29-capture-path.jsonl),
where a `FOLD` located exactly this caveat as the weakest leaf.

## Verify / replay

```bash
python3 recorder.py                              # self-test: build demo, verify, show the limit
python3 recorder.py --verify path/to/situation.jsonl
```

`verify()` replays the chain and catches reorder, edit, drop, and forward/unknown `refs` — the same
**re-derivation** MicroMoth-quilt gives a circuit ledger. If it re-derives every hash, the transcript
is a faithful record of how the manager related its parts, and the transcript is **attestable**: an
edit is expensive and a naive edit is named.

It is **not tamper-evident**, and the difference is not a wording preference. Re-derivation assumes
the tamperer does not recompute: re-chain an edit and the chain verifies perfectly; truncate the
tail and the remainder still verifies. Both need an external anchor, and this repo does not publish
one. The word for what holds here is *attestable*; see the house definition in
[`SuperInstance/witness-spec`](https://github.com/SuperInstance/witness-spec) `SPEC.md`.

## Why this is a cell, not a script

It has one job, a receipt, and a reproducible self-test, and it leaves a mark for the next agent —
so it composes. Directors emit a transcript per situation into `situations/transcripts/`; the prose
commit stays as the human time-capsule, the transcript is the machine-readable one beside it. As
transcripts accumulate they become the training set for the *learned dispatch router* and the
*decomposer* of [`../../situations/arch/ML-IN-THE-LOOP.md`](../../situations/arch/ML-IN-THE-LOOP.md) —
the fleet modeling itself as a thing.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""draw_local.py — un-gameable-shaped DRAW values from MicroMoth-quilt, no network.

When the Moth QRNG API is rate-limited, balance-gated, or CF-blocked, a captain
still needs `DRAW` records. This bridge gets them from a LOCAL MicroMoth-quilt
circuit (github.com/SuperInstance/MicroMoth-quilt) — pure Python, no keys, no
network — and seals each draw as a collapse-ledger receipt (attestable,
replayable). Feed the (value, receipt) straight into recorder.Situation.draw().

ATTESTABLE, not tamper-evident: the receipt's cell ids re-derive (so a naive
edit is named), but nothing is signed and no head is published out of band, so
a re-chained rewrite or a truncated receipt chain would still verify. The
MicroMoth-quilt lane this draws from makes the same claim, correctly:
github.com/SuperInstance/MicroMoth-quilt docs/ATTESTATION.md.

HONESTY (this matters — it keeps the corpus clean): MicroMoth-quilt is a
SIMULATOR. A seeded draw is quantum-STRUCTURED and REPLAYABLE with a hash-chained
receipt, but it is NOT a hardware QRNG and carries no Bell-S. So the provenance is
"micromoth-quilt/simulated (replayable, not hardware)". Use it as forced,
un-steerable-by-the-crew, reproducible exploration in-environment; reach for the
real Moth QRNG when you need hardware un-gameability. Never launder one as the other.

Locate MicroMoth-quilt via $MICROMOTH_QUILT (a clone path), else a sibling
../MicroMoth-quilt. Run directly for a self-demo:

    MICROMOTH_QUILT=/path/to/MicroMoth-quilt python3 draw_local.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import os
import sys
from pathlib import Path


def _locate_micromoth() -> Path:
    cand = []
    env = os.environ.get("MICROMOTH_QUILT")
    if env:
        cand.append(Path(env))
    here = Path(__file__).resolve()
    cand += [here.parent.parent.parent.parent / "MicroMoth-quilt",  # sibling of the ai-writings clone
             Path("/tmp/mmq")]
    for p in cand:
        if (p / "micromoth.py").exists():
            return p
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        "MicroMoth-quilt not found. Set $MICROMOTH_QUILT to a clone of "
        "github.com/SuperInstance/MicroMoth-quilt (looked in: %s)"
        % ", ".join(str(c) for c in cand))


def draw_int(min_v: int, max_v: int, seed: int = 0, qubits: int = 4, shots: int = 256,
             path: str | None = None) -> tuple[int, dict]:
    """Draw an integer in [min_v, max_v) from a local MicroMoth-quilt circuit.

    Circuit: `qubits` independent Hadamard coins (each qubit in equal
    superposition, measured) — the standard unbiased bit source. Seeded so the
    collapse receipt is SEALED and re-executable. The integer is rejection-sampled
    from the measured bitstream so it is uniform over [min_v, max_v). Returns
    (value, receipt) where receipt carries the collapse-ledger id + a balance stat
    (fraction of 1s ≈ 0.5 is the honest 'is the source fair' evidence, the local
    analogue of Moth's Bell-S) + honest provenance.
    """
    if max_v <= min_v:
        raise ValueError("max_v must exceed min_v")
    mm = _locate_micromoth() if path is None else Path(path)
    sys.path.insert(0, str(mm))
    sys.path.insert(0, str(mm / "tools"))
    import micromoth  # noqa: E402
    from collapse_ledger import collapse_receipt, verify  # noqa: E402

    qc = micromoth.QuantumCircuit(qubits, qubits)
    for q in range(qubits):
        qc.h(q)
    for q in range(qubits):
        qc.measure(q, q)

    receipt = collapse_receipt(qc, shots=shots, seed=seed)
    chk = verify(receipt, qc)
    if not chk.get("ok"):
        raise RuntimeError("collapse receipt failed self-verify: %s" % chk.get("why"))

    # Flatten the measured shots into one bitstream (strip spaces micromoth may insert).
    bits = "".join(str(o).replace(" ", "") for o in receipt["outcomes"])
    ones = sum(1 for b in bits if b == "1")
    balance = round(ones / len(bits), 4) if bits else None

    span = max_v - min_v
    width = max(1, math.ceil(math.log2(span)))
    value = None
    for i in range(0, len(bits) - width + 1, width):  # rejection sampling → uniform
        n = int(bits[i:i + width], 2)
        if n < span:
            value = min_v + n
            break
    if value is None:  # astronomically unlikely with these defaults
        raise RuntimeError("bitstream exhausted before an in-range draw; raise shots")

    last_cell = receipt["cells"][-1]["id"]
    summary = {
        "source": "micromoth-quilt/simulated (replayable, not hardware)",
        "collapse_ledger": last_cell,          # the sealed receipt id (chain head of the collapse EFFECTs)
        "dialect": receipt["dialect"],
        "sealed": receipt["sealed"],
        "seed": seed,
        "circuit": "%dxH+measure" % qubits,
        "shots": shots,
        "balance": balance,                     # ≈0.5 ⇒ unbiased; the local 'fair source' evidence
        "range": [min_v, max_v],
    }
    return value, summary


def main() -> int:
    v, r = draw_int(0, 10, seed=42)
    print("drew %d in [0,10)" % v)
    print("receipt:", r)
    assert r["sealed"] is True, "seeded draw must be sealed/replayable"
    v2, _ = draw_int(0, 10, seed=42)
    assert v == v2, "sealed draw must be reproducible under the same seed"
    print("reproducible under seed 42 ✓  (balance %.3f — ≈0.5 is fair)" % r["balance"])
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""recorder.py — turn a manager↔crew situation into a hash-chained transcript.

The fleet's real product is not only the repos a crew ships; it is the
*recorded inputs and outputs of the manager↔crew system* — a decomposable
corpus so a future model can learn to do what the manager does: take a
compound thing apart, locate where the value/truth lives, recombine. See
situations/arch/INTER-RELATIONAL-INTELLIGENCE.md for the why.

This is that capture unit, made small and reusable. One SITUATION is one
manager+crew mission (a dispatch). Its transcript is an append-only JSONL
receipt ledger — the SAME idiom github.com/SuperInstance/MicroMoth-quilt uses
for quantum circuits: every line a cell, chained, replayable. The v0 hash
algebra here was byte-compatible with that repo's tools/collapse_ledger.py on
purpose (one fewer idiom to invent; one more relationship made explicit
between two cells of the fleet).

ATTESTABLE, NOT TAMPER-EVIDENT. The chain re-derives, so an edit is expensive
and a naive edit is named — that is one leg of the three an anchor needs. The
head is not signed, and no head is published where the writer does not
control it. So a re-chained rewrite verifies perfectly, and a TRUNCATED chain
is a SHORTER VALID CHAIN: drop the last 50 records of a 121-record transcript
and verify() returns ok on the remaining 71. Nothing but an external anchor
fixes that. See sign_head() below and the house vocabulary in
github.com/SuperInstance/witness-spec SPEC.md ("Linkage class" and
"Tamper-evidence — the three legs").

Each line is a RELATION-record (the graph edges are its `refs`):

    envelope: sid, seq, ts, actor{tier,id,session}, rel, refs[], hash
    rel ∈ TASK ROUTE DRAFT DRAW FOLD KEEP DROP MARK OUTCOME

Zero dependencies (Python stdlib only), like micromoth.py. Run it directly for
a self-test that builds a demo situation and re-verifies the whole chain:

    python3 recorder.py            # -> writes example_situation.jsonl, verifies, prints OK
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import hashlib
import hmac
import json
import sys
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path


# ── witness-chain/1 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# The chain rule was upgraded. The old one is witness-chain/0 and is still
# READ and VERIFIED, because a log that cannot verify its own history is a
# lie about the past. New records are witness-chain/1.
#
#   v0:  hash = fnv1a64(json.dumps({prev, **envelope}, sort_keys=True,
#                                 separators=(",", ":")))
#   v1:  leaf(i) = SHA256(0x00 || JCS(record_i))
#        hash(i) = SHA256(0x01 || hash(i-1) || leaf(i))
#
# THREE REASONS, and the third is the important one.
#
# 1. RFC 8785 (JCS) instead of a house convention. The v0 canonicalisation
#    was json.dumps(sort_keys=True), reimplemented by hand in every port.
#    It is not a standard, and it DIVERGES from JCS in three measured ways:
#      * 1.0 -> "1.0" in v0, "1" in JCS (ECMAScript Number::toString)
#      * keys are sorted by CODE POINT in Python and by UTF-16 CODE UNIT in
#        JCS, so they disagree for any key above U+FFFF against one below
#      * Python's ensure_ascii escapes non-ASCII; JCS does not
#    RFC 8785 is a MUST in A2A v1.0 8.4.1, so this is interoperability too.
#
# 2. DOMAIN SEPARATION (RFC 6962 2.1): a leaf hashes with a 0x00 prefix and
#    a node with 0x01, so the two kinds of thing cannot be confused.
#
# 3. THE ONE THAT MATTERS: v0 HAD NO TAMPER-EVIDENCE.
#    A hash chain is SELF-CONSISTENT, and self-consistency is not
#    tamper-evidence. Rewrite a record, re-chain it, and the chain still
#    verifies -- because the attacker recomputed it. v0 also used FNV-1a-64,
#    which is 64 bits and not collision-resistant, so an attacker rewriting
#    a chain does not need to collide anything.
#    Tamper-evidence needs an anchor OUTSIDE the log: a SIGNED TREE HEAD,
#    signed under a key the log writer does not hold (RFC 6962 / Trillian's
#    LogWitness). See sign_head()/verify_head() below.
#
# The key must NOT be the log writer's key, or the writer can re-sign and
# there is no anchor. HMAC-SHA256 is used here because it is in both the
# Python and the JavaScript standard libraries; it is a STAND-IN, not a
# signature, because it is symmetric -- it proves "someone with the key
# wrote it", not "who". Ed25519 is the production answer.

CHAIN_VERSION = "witness-chain/1"
CHAIN_V1 = "witness-chain/1"
CHAIN_V0 = "witness-chain/0"

_LEAF_PREFIX = b"\x00"
_NODE_PREFIX = b"\x01"
_HEAD_PREFIX = b"\x03"


def _jcs_key(s: str) -> bytes:
    """Sort key: the key's UTF-16 code units, as bytes.

    JCS sorts object keys by UTF-16 CODE UNITS. Python's sorted() sorts by
    CODE POINT. They disagree for any key above U+FFFF against one below:

        "\U00010000"  code point 0x10000, UTF-16 lead unit 0xD800
        "\ue000"      code point 0xE000,  UTF-16 unit      0xE000

    Python's sorted() puts \ue000 first (0xE000 < 0x10000). UTF-16 puts
    \U00010000 first (0xD800 < 0xE000). So a chain hashed in Python and a
    chain hashed in JavaScript would diverge on any object carrying both
    kinds of key -- silently, and only on the keys that matter least.
    """
    return s.encode("utf-16-be", "surrogatepass")


_JCS_ESCAPES = {
    "\b": "\\b", "\t": "\\t", "\n": "\\n", "\f": "\\f", "\r": "\\r",
    '"': '\\"', "\\": "\\\\",
}


def _jcs_string(s: str) -> str:
    out = ['"']
    for ch in s:
        if ch in _JCS_ESCAPES:
            out.append(_JCS_ESCAPES[ch])
        elif ord(ch) < 0x20:
            out.append("\\u%04x" % ord(ch))
        else:
            out.append(ch)
    out.append('"')
    return "".join(out)


def _shortest_digits(v: float):
    """The shortest round-trip digits of a positive finite double.

    Returns (s, k, n) with value == s * 10**(n-k), 10**(k-1) <= s < 10**k,
    and k as small as possible. ECMA-262 6.1.6.1.20.
    """
    r = repr(v)                       # shortest round-trip, Python's layout
    if "e" in r or "E" in r:
        mant, _, exp = r.replace("E", "e").partition("e")
        exp = int(exp)
    else:
        mant, exp = r, 0
    ip, _, fp = mant.partition(".")
    digits = ip + fp
    n = len(ip) + exp                  # the decimal point sits after n digits
    stripped = digits.lstrip("0")
    n -= (len(digits) - len(stripped))
    digits = stripped.rstrip("0")
    if not digits:
        return ("0", 1, 1)
    return (digits, len(digits), n)


def _jcs_number(v: float) -> str:
    """ECMAScript Number::toString, exactly as RFC 8785 Appendix B wants.

    THE PREVIOUS VERSION OF THIS FUNCTION WAS WRONG, and it was wrong in the
    exact way the fleet's own witness-spec caught: it used Python's repr()
    with an exponent fix-up, and repr() is not ECMAScript's Number::toString.

    Three differences, each visible in RFC 8785 Appendix B:

      * the SHORTEST round-trip digits of a large integer are NOT the exact
        integer value. 295147905179352830000 is a double whose exact value
        is 295147905179352825856; ECMAScript prints the former.
      * the plain-decimal band is -6 < n <= 21, so 1e-6 prints as
        "0.000001", not "1e-06".
      * an exponent has NO leading zero: "9.999999999999997e-7".

    A chain is only worth its hash if the canonical form is the STANDARD
    one. The witness-spec conformance suite exists to catch exactly this,
    and it caught it here.
    """
    if v != v or v in (float("inf"), float("-inf")):
        raise ValueError("JCS: non-finite number")
    if v == 0:
        return "0"                      # -0 canonicalises to 0
    sign = "-" if v < 0 else ""
    s, k, n = _shortest_digits(abs(v))
    if k <= n <= 21:
        return sign + s + ("0" * (n - k))
    if 0 < n <= 21:
        return sign + s[:n] + "." + s[n:]
    if -6 < n <= 0:
        return sign + "0." + ("0" * (-n)) + s
    e = n - 1
    esign = "+" if e >= 0 else "-"
    head = s[0] if k == 1 else s[0] + "." + s[1:]
    return sign + head + "e" + esign + str(abs(e))


def _jcs(v) -> str:
    if v is None:
        return "null"
    if v is True:
        return "true"
    if v is False:
        return "false"
    if isinstance(v, str):
        return _jcs_string(v)
    if isinstance(v, int):
        # RFC 8785 s3.2.2.3 serializes a number as ECMAScript's
        # Number::toString -- that is, as the IEEE-754 DOUBLE. An integer
        # above 2^53 is not exactly representable as a double, so there is
        # no correct ECMAScript rendering OF THE VALUE: the only thing
        # ECMAScript can print is the value it would have ROUNDED TO.
        #
        # THIS IS NOT A COSMETIC EDGE. Python's json keeps an integer above
        # 2^53 EXACT through a round trip; JSON.parse in JavaScript cannot
        # represent it and rounds it to 9007199254740992. So the two
        # languages would hash the SAME logical record DIFFERENTLY -- and
        # 2^53+1 is not an I-JSON value, so RFC 8785 does not say which is
        # right. Found by cross-checking the two implementations against each
        # other for the first time.
        #
        # THE FIX IS NOT TO PICK A SIDE. A body that leaves the I-JSON range
        # must be REFUSED, so that the chain says "this cannot be hashed"
        # instead of quietly meaning something different in each language.
        if abs(v) > 9007199254740992:
            raise ValueError(
                "JCS: integer " + str(v) + " is outside the I-JSON range "
                "(+/- 2^53). It is not exactly representable as an IEEE-754 "
                "double, so ECMAScript's Number::toString -- which RFC 8785 "
                "requires -- has no correct rendering of it, and Python and "
                "JavaScript would canonicalize it differently. Refuse it "
                "rather than let two implementations disagree about what a "
                "record means. Store it as a string, or as a float, if the "
                "exact value matters.")
        return str(v)
    if isinstance(v, float):
        return _jcs_number(v)
    if isinstance(v, (list, tuple)):
        return "[" + ",".join(_jcs(x) for x in v) + "]"
    if isinstance(v, dict):
        keys = sorted(v.keys(), key=_jcs_key)
        return "{" + ",".join(_jcs_string(k) + ":" + _jcs(v[k]) for k in keys) + "}"
    raise TypeError("JCS: unsupported type " + type(v).__name__)


def _leaf_hash_v1(record: dict) -> str:
    body = {k: v for k, v in record.items() if k != "hash"}
    return "0x" + hashlib.sha256(_LEAF_PREFIX + _jcs(body).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()


def _chain_hash_v1(prev: str, leaf: str) -> str:
    return "0x" + hashlib.sha256(
        _NODE_PREFIX + prev.encode("utf-8") + leaf.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()


def sign_head(head: str, key: bytes) -> str:
    """The signed tree head -- the EXTERNAL ANANCHOR.

    Publish this somewhere the log writer does not control, and keep the key
    from the log writer. Without both, there is no anchor and no
    tamper-evidence, only a self-consistent chain.
    """
    return "0x" + hmac.new(key, _HEAD_PREFIX + head.encode("utf-8"), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()


def verify_head(head: str, signature: str, key: bytes) -> bool:
    return hmac.compare_digest(sign_head(head, key), signature)



# -- RFC 8785 Appendix B: the COMPLETE number-serialization samples -------

# The value is reconstructed from its IEEE-754 hex, so the test is
# self-contained and exact.
#
# This list was ADDED because the previous canonicalisation -- Python's

# These are ALL of them, asserted by COUNT, by hex, and by canonical form.
RFC8785_APPENDIX_B = [
    ("0000000000000000", "0"),
    ("8000000000000000", "0"),
    ("0000000000000001", "5e-324"),
    ("8000000000000001", "-5e-324"),
    ("7fefffffffffffff", "1.7976931348623157e+308"),
    ("ffefffffffffffff", "-1.7976931348623157e+308"),
    ("4340000000000000", "9007199254740992"),
    ("c340000000000000", "-9007199254740992"),
    ("4430000000000000", "295147905179352830000"),
    ("44b52d02c7e14af5", "9.999999999999997e+22"),
    ("44b52d02c7e14af6", "1e+23"),
    ("44b52d02c7e14af7", "1.0000000000000001e+23"),
    ("444b1ae4d6e2ef4e", "999999999999999700000"),
    ("444b1ae4d6e2ef4f", "999999999999999900000"),
    ("444b1ae4d6e2ef50", "1e+21"),
    ("3eb0c6f7a0b5ed8c", "9.999999999999997e-7"),

    ("41b3de4355555556", "333333333.3333334"),
    ("41b3de4355555557", "333333333.33333343"),

def _check_rfc8785() -> None:
    """Assert this implementation matches RFC 8785 Appendix B, in full."""
    import struct
    assert len(RFC8785_APPENDIX_B) == 24, (
        "RFC 8785 Appendix B has 24 numeric samples; this list has "
        + str(len(RFC8785_APPENDIX_B))
        + ". A truncated list is how the last bug hid.")
    for hexbits, want in RFC8785_APPENDIX_B:
        value = struct.unpack(">d", bytes.fromhex(hexbits))[0]
        got = _jcs(value)
        assert got == want, (
            "JCS disagrees with RFC 8785 Appendix B at " + hexbits
            + ": got " + repr(got) + " want " + repr(want))

    # THE I-JSON BOUNDARY, and the refusal that enforces it. Without this
    # check the behaviour is UNTESTED, and an untested refusal is a
    # comment: the next person to touch _jcs() would not know it was there.
    #
    # 2^53 is INSIDE the range and must canonicalize normally.
    assert _jcs(9007199254740992) == "9007199254740992", "2^53 is representable and must canonicalize"
    assert _jcs(-9007199254740992) == "-9007199254740992", "-2^53 likewise"
    # 2^53+1 is OUTSIDE it, and must be refused rather than canonicalized.
    for bad in (9007199254740993, -9007199254740993, 10 ** 30):
        try:
            got = _jcs(bad)
        except ValueError:
            continue
        raise AssertionError(
            "JCS accepted the out-of-range integer " + str(bad) + " and "
            "canonicalized it to " + repr(got) + ". Two implementations "
            "would disagree about that record and no spec says which is "
            "right. It must be refused.")
    # A bool is an int in Python, and must NOT be refused.
    assert _jcs(True) == "true" and _jcs(False) == "false"


GENESIS = "0x0000000000000000"
REL_TYPES = {"TASK", "ROUTE", "DRAFT", "DRAW", "FOLD", "KEEP", "DROP", "MARK", "OUTCOME"}


def fnv1a64(s: str) -> int:
    """fnv1a-64 over utf-8 — the fleet WAL convention (matches MicroMoth-quilt)."""
    h = 0xCBF29CE484222325
    for b in s.encode("utf-8"):
        h ^= b
        h = (h * 0x100000001B3) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
    return h


def _canon(obj) -> str:
    return json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))


def _now() -> str:
    return datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")


class Situation:
    """An append-only, hash-chained transcript of one manager↔crew mission.

    The chain rule mirrors MicroMoth-quilt's cell id: each record's `hash` is
    a commitment over the previous record's hash and this record's body. So
    the transcript is replayable: recompute the chain from the bodies and it
    must reproduce every hash, or a record was edited or reordered.

    That is RE-DERIVATION (leg 1 of 3), and it is what "chain-intact" means.
    It is not tamper-evidence: an attacker who recomputes the chain over their
    own edit re-derives perfectly, and a truncated transcript is a shorter
    valid chain. See the module docstring.
    """

    def __init__(self, sid: str, ts=None):
        self.sid = sid
        self.records: list[dict] = []
        self._clock = ts  # optional callable for deterministic timestamps (tests)

    # --- core ---------------------------------------------------------------

    def emit(self, rel: str, actor: dict, body: dict, refs=None) -> dict:
        """Append one relation-record and return it (with its computed hash)."""
        if rel not in REL_TYPES:
            raise ValueError("unknown rel %r (allowed: %s)" % (rel, sorted(REL_TYPES)))
        if not isinstance(actor, dict) or "tier" not in actor:
            raise ValueError("actor must be a dict with at least a 'tier' key")
        prev = self.records[-1]["hash"] if self.records else GENESIS
        rec = {
            "v": CHAIN_VERSION,
            "sid": self.sid,
            "seq": len(self.records),
            "ts": (self._clock() if self._clock else _now()),
            "actor": actor,
            "rel": rel,
            "refs": list(refs or []),
            "body": body,
        }
        rec["hash"] = _chain_hash_v1(prev, _leaf_hash_v1(rec))
        self.records.append(rec)
        return rec

    # --- typed convenience verbs (the inter-relational primitives) ----------

    def task(self, actor, brief, refs=None):
        return self.emit("TASK", actor, {"brief": brief}, refs)

    def route(self, actor, subtask, to, why, refs=None):
        return self.emit("ROUTE", actor, {"subtask": subtask, "to": to, "why": why}, refs)

    def draft(self, actor, prompt, response, params=None, refs=None):
        return self.emit("DRAFT", actor,
                         {"prompt": prompt, "response": response, "params": params or {}}, refs)

    def draw(self, actor, request, value, receipt, refs=None):
        """An un-gameable draw. `receipt` carries provenance: a Moth Bell-S, OR a
        MicroMoth-quilt collapse-ledger id when drawing locally in-environment."""
        return self.emit("DRAW", actor,
                         {"request": request, "value": value, "receipt": receipt}, refs)

    def fold(self, actor, claim, leaves, refs=None):
        """The decomposition record. `leaves` is a list of {claim, verdict}. We store
        the located weakest (argmin) and the GAP the single number would have hidden —
        the datum that teaches how much a scalar verdict smoothed over."""
        if not leaves:
            raise ValueError("fold needs at least one leaf")
        verdicts = [float(l["verdict"]) for l in leaves]
        argmin = min(range(len(leaves)), key=lambda i: verdicts[i])
        folded = min(verdicts)  # the weakest leaf is the honest ceiling of the conjunction
        whole = None
        for l in leaves:
            if l.get("is_whole"):
                whole = float(l["verdict"])
        body = {
            "claim": claim,
            "leaves": leaves,
            "weakest_index": argmin,
            "weakest_claim": leaves[argmin].get("claim"),
            "folded_min": folded,
            "whole_verdict": whole,
            "gap": (None if whole is None else round(folded - whole, 6)),
        }
        return self.emit("FOLD", actor, body, refs)

    def keep(self, actor, candidate_ref, reason, refs=None):
        r = list(refs or [])
        if candidate_ref not in r:
            r.append(candidate_ref)
        return self.emit("KEEP", actor, {"candidate": candidate_ref, "reason": reason}, r)

    def drop(self, actor, candidate_ref, reason, refs=None):
        r = list(refs or [])
        if candidate_ref not in r:
            r.append(candidate_ref)
        return self.emit("DROP", actor, {"candidate": candidate_ref, "reason": reason}, r)

    def mark(self, actor, kind, ref, refs=None):
        """A durable artifact written (commit sha / doc path / receipt id)."""
        return self.emit("MARK", actor, {"kind": kind, "ref": ref}, refs)

    def outcome(self, actor, of_ref, result, detail=None, refs=None):
        """A realized downstream result (CI green/red, revert, measured speedup) —
        the delayed label. `of_ref` points back at the record it judges."""
        r = list(refs or [])
        if of_ref not in r:
            r.append(of_ref)
        return self.emit("OUTCOME", actor, {"of": of_ref, "result": result, "detail": detail}, r)

    # --- persistence + verification ----------------------------------------

    def to_jsonl(self) -> str:
        return "".join(_canon(r) + "\n" for r in self.records)

    def write(self, path):
        Path(path).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        Path(path).write_text(self.to_jsonl(), encoding="utf-8")
        return path


def _envelope(rec: dict) -> dict:
    """The record without its own hash — what the chain commits to."""
    return {k: v for k, v in rec.items() if k != "hash"}


def verify(records) -> tuple[bool, str]:
    """Replay the chain. Returns (ok, message). Catches reorder, edit, and drop.

    BOTH chain versions are accepted, and a chain that MIXES them is a
    FAILURE, not a convenience:

      witness-chain/0  fnv1a64 over a house-convention canonical form
      witness-chain/1  SHA-256, RFC 8785 canonicalisation, RFC 6962 domain
                       separation

    The version is a field INSIDE the record, so it is inside the hashed
    bytes: you cannot strip or downgrade a version without breaking the
    chain. That is why a mixed chain is detectable.

    What this does NOT do: it does not detect an edit that the writer
    RE-CHAINED. A chain is self-consistent, and self-consistency is not
    tamper-evidence. For that you need the signed tree head -- sign_head()
    and verify_head() -- published somewhere the writer does not control.
    """
    prev = GENESIS
    seen_version = None
    for i, rec in enumerate(records):
        if rec.get("seq") != i:
            return False, "seq gap at index %d (got %r)" % (i, rec.get("seq"))
        version = rec.get("v")
        if version is None:
            version = CHAIN_V0
        if seen_version is None:
            seen_version = version
        elif version != seen_version:
            return False, ("MIXED CHAIN VERSIONS at seq %d: %s then %s -- a chain "
                           "does not change its rule mid-flight; start a new "
                           "transcript and name the previous head in it"
                           % (i, seen_version, version))
        if version == CHAIN_V1:
            want = _chain_hash_v1(prev, _leaf_hash_v1(rec))
        else:
            want = "0x%016x" % fnv1a64(_canon({"prev": prev, **_envelope(rec)}))
        if rec.get("hash") != want:
            return False, "hash mismatch at seq %d: stored %s want %s" % (
                i, rec.get("hash"), want)
        for ref in rec.get("refs", []):
            if isinstance(ref, str) and ref.startswith("0x") and ref not in {
                    r["hash"] for r in records[:i]}:
                return False, "seq %d refs unknown/forward hash %s" % (i, ref)
        prev = rec["hash"]
    # "chain-intact" means precisely THE CHAIN VERIFIED. It is not a claim
    # about tampering: this same function returns ok for a tail-truncated
    # chain, because a prefix of a valid chain is a valid chain. Leg 1 of 3
    # only -- re-derived, not anchored. See the module docstring.
    return True, ("ok: %d records, chain-intact (%s) "
                  "[leg 1 of 3: re-derived, not anchored -- not tamper-evident]"
                  % (len(records), seen_version or CHAIN_V0))


def head(records) -> str:
    """The chain head -- what gets signed."""
    return records[-1]["hash"] if records else GENESIS


def load(path) -> list[dict]:
    return [json.loads(line) for line in Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines() if line]


# --- self-test / demo -------------------------------------------------------

def _demo() -> Situation:
    """Build a small but real-shaped situation: a captain routes a claim-check to a
    crew member, draws an adversary locally (MicroMoth-quilt), folds the crew's
    compound claim through the referee, drops it on the located weakest leaf, and
    books the scar. Deterministic timestamps so the demo file is reproducible."""
    ticks = iter(["2026-09-29T05:20:%02dZ" % s for s in range(0, 40, 3)])
    s = Situation("sit-demo-0001", ts=lambda: next(ticks))
    disp = {"tier": "dispatcher", "id": "opus-4.8", "session": "parent"}
    cap = {"tier": "captain", "id": "opus-5.5", "session": "fresh-01"}
    crew = {"tier": "crew", "id": "deepseek-chat", "session": "fresh-01"}
    ref = {"tier": "referee", "id": "jev-latest", "session": "fresh-01"}
    dice = {"tier": "dice", "id": "micromoth-quilt/bell", "session": "fresh-01"}

    t = s.task(disp, "Verify the crew's anatomy claim before it lands in a README.")
    r = s.route(cap, "fact-check compound claim", to="deepseek-chat",
                why="cheap hauler; captain reserves judgment for the fold", refs=[t["hash"]])
    d = s.draft(crew,
                prompt="State four facts about the human heart.",
                response=("four chambers; pumps blood; contains the SA node; "
                          "located entirely on the left side of the chest"),
                refs=[r["hash"]])
    dr = s.draw(dice, request="draw adversary leaf index in [0,4)",
                value=3,
                receipt={"collapse_ledger": "0x… (micromoth-quilt bell, local, no network)",
                         "note": "un-gameable in-env: quantum-shaped, nobody steered it"},
                refs=[d["hash"]])
    f = s.fold(ref,
               claim="the heart claim (compound)",
               leaves=[
                   {"claim": "the compound claim as a whole", "verdict": 0.11, "is_whole": True},
                   {"claim": "four chambers", "verdict": 0.98},
                   {"claim": "pumps blood through the body", "verdict": 0.97},
                   {"claim": "contains the SA node that sets rhythm", "verdict": 0.95},
                   {"claim": "located entirely on the left side of the chest", "verdict": 0.08},
               ],
               refs=[d["hash"], dr["hash"]])
    dp = s.drop(cap, candidate_ref=d["hash"],
                reason=("fold located the rot at leaf 3 (left-side), the same leaf the "
                        "un-gameable draw hit; whole-verdict 0.11 hid WHERE — gap %.2f"
                        % f["body"]["gap"]),
                refs=[f["hash"]])
    m = s.mark(cap, kind="ledger", ref="dispatch-ledger.csv#d121", refs=[dp["hash"]])
    s.outcome(disp, of_ref=m["hash"], result="scar-booked",
              detail="claim kept OUT of the README; transcript retained as a FOLD example",
              refs=[f["hash"]])
    return s


def main(argv=None):
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="situation-recorder self-test / verifier")
    ap.add_argument("--verify", metavar="PATH", help="verify an existing transcript JSONL")
    ap.add_argument("--out", default=str(Path(__file__).with_name("example_situation.jsonl")),
                    help="where the demo writes its transcript")
    args = ap.parse_args(argv)

    if args.verify:
        ok, msg = verify(load(args.verify))
        print(("VERIFY OK  — " if ok else "VERIFY FAIL — ") + msg)
        return 0 if ok else 1

    _check_rfc8785()
    print("RFC 8785 Appendix B: all 24 samples match")

    s = _demo()
    path = s.write(args.out)
    ok, msg = verify(s.records)
    assert ok, msg
    # naive-edit check: flipping one field must break the chain downstream.
    # NAIVE -- an attacker who recomputes the chain over their own edit
    # passes this, which is the limit the next block demonstrates.
    bad = load(path)
    bad[3]["body"]["value"] = 0
    tampered_ok, _ = verify(bad)
    assert not tampered_ok, "tamper went undetected — chain is not doing its job"
    print("wrote %s (%d records)" % (path, len(s.records)))
    print(msg)
    print("re-derivation: editing seq 3 breaks verification ✓ (a naive edit)")

    # ── the honest limits, demonstrated ────────────────────────────────────
    #
    # A chain is SELF-CONSISTENT. An attacker who edits a record and
    # RE-CHAINS it produces a chain that verifies perfectly -- and the
    # difference between "nobody touched this" and "somebody rewrote the
    # whole thing" is INVISIBLE without an anchor outside the log.
    #
    # This is the defect the old rule (witness-chain/0) had, and it is worth
    # being able to SHOW rather than assert.
    key = b"a-key-the-log-writer-does-not-hold"
    good = load(path)
    sig = sign_head(head(good), key)

    forged = load(path)
    forged[3]["body"]["value"] = 0
    # The attacker recomputes the chain over their own edit -- and must also
    # re-point every `refs` entry that names a hash they changed, because
    # verify() checks refs against the hashes of EARLIER records. Re-pointing
    # a ref changes a record's body, which changes its hash, which cascades.
    # So the attack is a FIXPOINT, and this iterates it to convergence.
    #
    # (A first attempt that only re-chained, without re-pointing refs, was
    # caught -- by the refs check. That is a SECOND layer of detection, and
    # it is worth knowing about, but it is not the same as tamper-evidence:
    # it is only as good as the attacker's care. The signed head does not
    # depend on the attacker's competence.)
    for _ in range(16):
        before = [r["hash"] for r in forged]
        prev = GENESIS
        for r in forged:
            r["hash"] = _chain_hash_v1(prev, _leaf_hash_v1(r))
            prev = r["hash"]
        remap = {before[i]: forged[i]["hash"] for i in range(len(forged))}
        changed = False
        for r in forged:
            for j, ref in enumerate(r.get("refs", [])):
                if isinstance(ref, str) and ref in remap and remap[ref] != ref:
                    r["refs"][j] = remap[ref]
                    changed = True
        if not changed:
            break
    forged_ok, forged_msg = verify(forged)
    print("RE-CHAINED rewrite verifies?           %s  (%s)" % (forged_ok, forged_msg))
    print("  -> a chain alone CANNOT tell. The witness log is self-consistent,")
    print("     not tamper-evident. That was true of witness-chain/0 too.")
    anchored_ok = verify_head(head(forged), sig, key)
    print("RE-CHAINED rewrite caught by the signed head? %s" % (not anchored_ok))
    assert forged_ok, "expected a re-chained rewrite to still verify -- if this fails, the demo is not showing the real limit"
    assert not anchored_ok, "the signed head did NOT catch a re-chained rewrite -- the anchor is broken"
    print("with a signed head, a re-chained rewrite is CAUGHT ✓")
    print("  NOTE: that is legs 1+2. It is NOT yet tamper-evident -- the head")
    print("  must also be PUBLISHED where the writer cannot control it, and")
    print("  no such publication exists in this repo. Until it does, the")
    print("  honest word is 'attestable'. A signed head stored inside the log")
    print("  it anchors can be refreshed for free after any rewrite.")
    w = s.records[4]["body"]
    print("demo FOLD located weakest = leaf %d (%r), gap vs whole = %s"
          % (w["weakest_index"], w["weakest_claim"], w["gap"]))
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

# MicroMoth-quilt

**The smallest quantum computing framework, taught to keep receipts.**

This repo is two things, and this README says both up front:

   what if a quantum circuit *were* a hash-chained receipt ledger? Every gate
   a BIND cell, every measurement a sealed collapse event, every view a VIEW
   cell — fnv1a-64 chained, replayable, **attestable**.

   *Attestable*, not tamper-evident: the chain re-derives, so an edit is

   outside this repo, so a re-chained rewrite and a tail-truncation both

## Why receipts on a quantum simulator?

A quantum circuit is already almost a ledger: an ordered list of operations
ending in measurement events. The fleet's doctrine is that *every
computational act deserves a receipt it can be challenged with* — and quantum
adds a sharp reason: **collapse is an event, not a state**. A seeded collapse
receipt turns "this shot gave 01 under seed s" into a re-executable claim
instead of a number in a histogram. The design note
([`docs/CELL-MAPPING.md`](docs/CELL-MAPPING.md)) works this out op by op; the
short version: primitives, not sugar — `y`/`z`/`ry` decompose at append time,
so a circuit cell chain never contains them.

## Upstream README (preserved verbatim)

# MicroMoth

There are many well-developed and feature-rich frameworks for quantum computing. These allow quantum programs to be created and then run on either advanced simulators or real prototype quantum devices. Though it's obviously a good thing to have many features and support many use-cases, it can sometimes be too much of a good thing!

For this reason we present MicroMoth: the smallest and most feature-poor framework for quantum computing. It has all the basic features and only the basic features. Making it much easier to learn, and much easier to get running.

MicroMoth is an actively maintained fork of [MicroQiskit](https://github.com/qiskit-community/MicroQiskit), which was initially conceived as a version of the [Qiskit](https://www.ibm.com/quantum/qiskit) SDK that could run on microcontroller devices. The strict need for simplicity and a lack of complex dependencies was the main guidance for the design. MicroMoth has some additional features in comparison with the original MicroQiskit.

MicroMoth also contains ports for other languages, so you can bring the world of quantum into your familiar workflows. If you don't see your favourite language, note that it might be available for [MicroQiskit](versions/update_required) instead since we haven't finished upgrading all the ports.

### Template Version

The [micromoth.py](micromoth.py) file found in this folder is intended as a template version. It contains comments to explain how each part of MicroMoth works, both to aid understanding and to help in the writing of ports. The MicroPython version is directly constructed from this template.

### JavaScript / Web

* [JavaScript port](versions/JavaScript/micromoth.js) — a faithful, zero-dependency ES module port of the template, for the browser and Node. Same gates (`x`, `h`, `rx`, `rz`, and the `y`/`z`/`t`/`ry` gates built from them), same `cx`/`crx`/`swap` two-qubit gates (plus a `crz` extension, wired into the simulator the same way `crx` is), and the same measurement/`simulate()` semantics (`counts`, `memory`, `probability_dictionary`, `statevector`).
* [`quantum-wow/`](quantum-wow/) — a modular **"quantum wow" plugin** built on that port: a drop-in for quilt, cargo-line, qthe, or any other web project that wants a genuine quantum wow, click-and-play, with no key required.

#### `quantum-wow` plugin

`quantum-wow/quantum-wow.js` is a zero-dependency ES module exposing:

- **`quantumSeed(nbits = 32)`** — a random seed drawn from a real (simulated, by default) quantum circuit: `nbits` qubits put into superposition with Hadamard gates, then measured. Returns `{ seed, bits, mode, degraded }`.
- **`quantumCoin()`** — a single quantum coin flip (`{ result: 'heads'|'tails', bit, mode, degraded }`).
- **`quantumField(n = 8)`** — a small quantum-circuit-driven value field: `n` values in `[0, 1]`, cheap enough to drive a visual effect (a dot grid, a shimmer) without being a full engine.
- **A backend adapter with two modes, same interface:**
  - **`simulated` (default, no key)** — runs MicroMoth locally, right in the visitor's browser. This is the click-and-play, no-key wow.
  - **`real` (BYO key)** — when a visitor supplies their own [Moth Quantum](https://platform.mothquantum.com) API key, calls route to the real `comet-qrng-v1` engine (`https://api.mothquantum.com/api/v1`, async job: `POST /engines/comet-qrng-v1/process` → poll `GET /jobs/{id}/status` → `GET /jobs/{id}/result`), for genuine Born-rule measurements on IBM quantum hardware. **If the real call fails for any reason it degrades gracefully back to `simulated` and says so** — every public method always returns a usable result, plus `{ mode, degraded, error }` so the caller (or the bundled widget) can be honest about what actually happened. A key is never hardcoded: it's supplied by the visitor at runtime (`quantumWow.setApiKey(...)`), or, for a server deployment, resolved at call time from a `keyProvider` you wire to your own secrets store.
- **`mountWidget(container, quantumWow)`** — a small embeddable, framework-free, cream/ink-themed widget: a live "⚛️ quantum: simulated / real" status, a one-line explanation with a link placeholder, and a key-input field ("Have a Moth key? Paste it for real IBM-quantum results ↗") that flips the widget to real mode live and shows the degrade reason honestly if a real call doesn't go through.

`quantum-wow/index.html` is a click-and-play demo of all of the above — draw a seed, flip a coin, sample a field, then paste a key to try the real-hardware upgrade.

To drop this into another project (quilt, cargo-line, qthe, ...), copy the two files `quantum-wow/quantum-wow.js` and `quantum-wow/micromoth.js` into it (they're a self-contained pair — no bundler, no dependencies) and `import { QuantumWow, mountWidget } from './quantum-wow.js'`.

**Note on the "real" mode:** `api.mothquantum.com` does not currently send CORS headers, so a real-mode call made directly from client-side JS in a browser will be blocked by the browser itself (visible as a fast network-level failure, which the adapter treats like any other failure and degrades from) — a production deployment wanting the real upgrade to actually complete in-browser would route it through a small server-side proxy (a Cloudflare Pages Function/Worker), which is also where the `keyProvider`/secrets-store pattern is meant to be used. Separately, even server-to-server, the `comet-qrng-v1` engine's certified hardware (`mode: 'qpu'`) path can legitimately return zero extractable bytes for modest shot counts, since its NIST SP 800-90B extractor subtracts a large "ordering penalty" when the backend returns counts only (no per-shot memory) — that's a real, honest "no usable output" outcome from a job that did run for real on IBM hardware, not a bug, and it degrades the same way a scope/permission error would.
